newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Troubled Yugo banks seek better treatment.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Yugo banks seek better treatment.

text.p: Yugoslavia's leading bankers called on the government on Wednesday to help the troubled sector solve its problems instead of blaming it for widespread illiquidity and impotence of the entire economy.
They warned that monetary policy alone could not bring price and currency stability, let alone be sufficient for an economic progress.

"The situation in the banking sector is very difficult, but the state attempts to shift all problems onto banks while problems are of the entire economy," head of the Vojvodjanska banka Zivota Mihajlovic told a bankers' meeting.
"The state never criticises those parts of the economy responsible for increasing production, it's always and only banks," he said.
Mihajlovic said banks could not improve their performance in a country where debtors were protected instead of creditors.

"Banks are making losses, but nobody talks about companies making losses. It is high time the state became serious and gave banks the treatment they deserved," said Mihaljovic, who also chairs Banking Committee of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce.

Banks in Yugoslavia are blamed for the interest rates (running above 15 percent per month) they charge on commercial loans, which translate into high borrowing costs for firms and high prices of their products.
But bankers said their lending rates would go down once the state addressed the issue of collecting debts.

"Much of the interest rate's size reflects the risk bankers calculate when lending. But when the state starts protecting creditors, those rates will begin to fall," said Slobodan Vukovic, head of the Prva Preduzetnicka Banka.

Banks had no means to protect themselves and collect what they lent because of the strong debtors lobby, mainly from among the companies which counted on inflation and devaluation to minimize their debts.
Bankers urged the central bank to relax its stance on commercial banks and lower the reserve requirement.
"This would ease our daily routine, particularly if the NBY paid an interest rate equal to its discount rate on those funds," one banker said.
The reserve requirement was seen as the only instrument left for the central bank to regulate liquidity of the banking sector and control the M1 money supply.

Despite frequent pledges on tough monetary policy and reassurances that it was applying currency board mechanism in creating base money, NBY could not stop M1 money supply from exploding by around 70 percent in 1996.

According to data presented by the Banking Committee of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce, base money grew by 91.4 percent, while banks' dinar lending increased by 100.5 percent against 1995. Cash in circulation accounted for 55 percent of M1.

Even though it promised another year of austerity, the NBY was seen unable to keep the M1 at the level of 5.5 billion dinars where it stood at the end of 1996 or allow it to grow by exactly the same percentage of the GDP growth.
Yugoslavia's government planned a 13 percent GDP growth and a zero inflation in 1997. But a 1.4 percent monthly inflation in January already showed the plans were unrealistic.
The big problem of the Yugoslav economy lay with its huge $2.26 billion trade gap, which continued to rise early in 1997, without bringing the hoped for revival of domestic industry.

The country's forex reserves, unofficially estimated between $200 million and $300 million, were seen insufficient to protect the dinar, finance massive state administration, huge public spending and imports needed to enliven the economy in which 50 percent of production capacities were idle.
"Everything in this country is left to monetary policy. But except for the price stability, other goals must be a matter of wider macroeconomic policy.

"This central bank is in deep dilemma -- to base its monetary policy on the government economic targets or drop any official estimates and do the whole business on its own," said an economist who insisted not to be named. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
